analysis.one_liner: Replaces all federal income, payroll, and estate taxes with a 23% national sales tax plus monthly rebates.
analysis.headline: Despite 47 Republican cosponsors, the bill sat in the House Ways and Means Committee for the full two-year Congress without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the individual and corporate income taxes, the Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and the estate and gift taxes, and replace them with a single national sales tax of 23% (measured on a tax-inclusive basis) on all new goods and services. States that already run sales taxes would collect the federal tax and keep a small administration fee, and the IRS would be phased out of existence. Every lawful-resident family would get a monthly rebate covering the tax on poverty-level spending. If Congress did not repeal the Sixteenth Amendment within seven years, the sales tax would sunset.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households and large estates gain the most: the taxes that fall hardest on them — income tax on wages and investment returns and the estate tax — are abolished, and purchases made for investment purposes are explicitly untaxed, so money that sits in wealth accumulation is never taxed. Supporters argue everyone gains from the simplicity of one visible sales tax and that the monthly rebate shields the poorest families.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the individual income tax, corporate income tax, payroll and self-employment taxes, and estate and gift taxes, effective January 1, 2019.
Imposes a national sales tax of 23% in 2019 on the use or consumption of taxable property and services, collected by sellers and remitted through the states.

Gives every lawful-resident family a monthly 'Family Consumption Allowance' rebate equal to the tax rate times the federal poverty level for their family size, paid by the Social Security Administration.
Exempts used property, business purchases, investment purchases, exports, and state government functions from the tax.
Authorizes no funding for IRS operations after fiscal year 2021 and has states, not the federal government, administer the tax.
Terminates the national sales tax if the constitutional amendment authorizing the income tax is not repealed within seven years.

analysis.who_pays: Households that spend most of what they earn — typically middle-income families — pay the tax on everything they buy beyond the rebate-covered poverty level, and because the rate is flat on consumption while the repealed taxes were progressive, the tax burden shifts toward them relative to high earners. Future Social Security and Medicare beneficiaries also bear new risk: the payroll taxes that directly fund those programs are repealed and replaced by sales tax revenue allocated to the trust funds.

drawbacks.text: The stated 23% rate is measured on a tax-inclusive basis — a percentage of the total price including the tax — which corresponds to roughly a 30% addition on the pre-tax price of everything new that consumers buy.

Repealing the payroll taxes that directly fund Social Security and Medicare and replacing them with sales tax revenue makes the retirement and health programs dependent on consumer spending patterns and on future Congresses allocating general revenue to the trust funds.

Purchases for investment purposes and used property are untaxed, so income from wealth — capital gains, dividends, and large inheritances after estate tax repeal — escapes federal taxation entirely, while wages are taxed when spent.

Because a consumption tax is flat while the income tax was progressive, taxes rise as a share of income for households in the middle of the income distribution even after the rebate, while falling sharply at the top.

The rebate requires every family to register annually with the tax authority, list each member's Social Security number, and certify lawful residency, creating a new federal database of household information.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine gains — a simpler tax code, no income tax filing, and a rebate that protects poverty-level spending — are real but come packaged with a large structural shift: the progressive taxes on income and inherited wealth are repealed and replaced with a flat tax on spending. Middle-income households would pay more of their income in tax, high-income households and large estates would pay dramatically less, and the dedicated funding stream for Social Security and Medicare would be replaced with a less stable one. A bill designed only to simplify could have kept progressive rates; this one does not.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced in January 2017 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Rob Woodall introduced the FairTax Act of 2017 on January 3, 2017, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
The bill's only recorded actions in the entire 115th Congress were its introduction and its referral to Ways and Means; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever held.
47 House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing, more progressive tax code stayed in place, which — under the bill's own structure — means middle-income households avoided the tax increase they would have borne, the estate tax continued to apply to the largest inheritances, and the tax-preparation industry kept the revenue it would have lost with the income tax.

for.name: Rep. Rob Woodall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FairTax Act of 2017 on the first day of the 115th Congress and recruited cosponsors for it.

for.name: 47 of 241 House Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors in the House of Representatives

against.name: Rep. Kevin Brady
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its referral; the committee held no hearing or markup and the full House never voted on it during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 48 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, none of the chamber's 194 Democrats signed on, and the Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee let the bill die without action.

industries.note: The bill repeals the income tax (including tax on capital gains and dividends), the estate and gift taxes, and explicitly exempts investment purchases from the sales tax, so wealth accumulation would go untaxed. The revenue gap would be filled by a flat tax on consumption, which weighs heaviest on households that spend most of their income.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: Without an income tax and without the IRS, the market for filing services, compliance software, and audit defense disappears. The industry's interest ran against the bill, since its revenue depends on the complexity the bill would eliminate.

Retailers would collect the federal tax at the register and face new reporting duties, segregated deposit accounts, and bonding requirements for large sellers, but they receive an administration credit of up to a quarter of one percent of tax remitted and would pay no income or payroll tax themselves.

industries.industry: State governments with existing sales taxes
industries.note: States that sign cooperative agreements would become the permanent administrative channel for the federal tax, keeping a 0.25% administration fee, effectively replacing the IRS with state tax agencies.

industries.industry: Social Security and Medicare trust funds
industries.note: The bill repeals the dedicated payroll taxes that fund these programs and instead allocates a share of sales tax revenue to the trust funds, changing their funding from an earmarked payroll tax to a consumption-based stream that depends on future congressional action.
